title: Shot by ICE in New York, Man Faces Immigration Judge With Bullet Still in His Neck
excerpt: Oscar Belgal, 28, shot on October 8 with his 5-year-old son in the car, appeared by video from Brooklyn detention; a federal judge has temporarily barred his deportation.
body:
• Oscar Belgal, 28, a Dominican national, was shot by federal immigration officers in New York on October 8 while his 5-year-old son sat in the car; his lawyers say a bullet remains lodged in the back of his neck and he needs surgery.
  • He appeared in immigration court on October 15 by video from the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, barely speaking; his lawyers say he is on 24-hour lockdown with no phone access to family.
  • A federal judge has temporarily barred his deportation and ordered the government to explain why he should remain in mandatory detention; his next immigration hearing is October 29.
  • His lawyers say masked officers in civilian clothes never identified themselves before smashing his window and firing; DHS says officers fired only after he smashed his car into two government vehicles and accelerated toward them.

A New York man shot by federal immigration officers while his young son sat in the car appeared in immigration court on Thursday with a bullet still lodged in the back of his neck, the Associated Press reported. Oscar Belgal, 28, a native of the Dominican Republic, appeared remotely from the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn and barely spoke during the brief hearing before Judge Dara Reid.

Belgal was shot on October 8 in Manhattan. ICE officers confronted him while he was looking for a parking spot after picking up his 5-year-old son from school; the boy was in the car when an officer ran up and smashed one of its windows, according to AP.

Two Accounts of the Shooting

In a court filing on Wednesday, Belgal's lawyers at the Legal Aid Society said the officers wore masks and civilian clothes, never identified themselves, and fired several shots into the vehicle as he tried to drive away. They say he needs surgery to remove the bullet, has been given only ibuprofen for pain, and that the left side of his face is numb and his hearing in his left ear is impaired.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Ga5nVrTHtGE

The Department of Homeland Security gives a sharply different account: officials say the officers believed their lives were in danger and fired only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and accelerated toward them. Federal officials had previously described his injury as "superficial" — a description his lawyers' surgery claim directly contradicts. NYPD-released footage shows part of the encounter but does not conclusively show the shooting itself, AP reported.

Solitary Confinement and a Judge's Limits

Legal Aid attorney Karene Brown told the judge Belgal is on 24-hour lockdown — solitary confinement — with no phone access to his family, and that ICE has not honoured her request to move him. Judge Reid said she has no say over where he is housed inside the facility. Belgal tried to raise his living conditions during the hearing, but his lawyer advised him against it and cut him off, AP reported.

His lawyers have also filed a federal petition seeking his release. On Wednesday, a federal judge ordered the administration to explain why he should remain in custody and temporarily barred his deportation.

What Happens Next

Belgal's next immigration hearing is scheduled for October 29. Between now and then, the two disputes that define this case — what happened on that Manhattan street on October 8, and whether a man who says he needs surgery should be held in solitary confinement while it is decided — will be argued in two different courtrooms.
image_caption: Officers tend to Oscar Belgal after he was shot by federal immigration officers in New York on October 8, in NYPD body-camera footage released by the department. His lawyers say a bullet remains lodged in the back of his neck.
nri_angle: The case tests ICE use of force and detention conditions in front of two courts at once — a process immigrant families across the US follow closely.
author: Diaspora Desk
